arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Convenience Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 500 adult consumers in Germany and Switzerland, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income.
arguments.measure: 1) Purchase intent: "Would you buy this machine?" (binary: Yes/No). 2) WTP: "How much would you pay more than a comparable entry-level machine?" (WTP in euros). 3) Messaging preference: "Which attribute matters more to you?" (Quality vs Convenience).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium messaging will generate at least 15% higher purchase intent and higher WTP than convenience messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience messaging will generate at least 15% higher purchase intent and higher WTP than premium messaging.

arguments.decision_rule: If premium messaging yields purchase intent at least 15% higher than convenience messaging AND WTP difference is at least €10, proceed with a premium consumer proposition. If convenience messaging yields purchase intent at least 15% higher AND WTP difference is at least €10, proceed with a convenience-focused proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated premium consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home office) that emphasizes professional quality, convenience features, and modern design. Use the proposed Consumer Preference Test to validate whether premium messaging drives higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than convenience messaging before committing to full development and marketing.

frame.objective: Determine whether Franke Coffee Systems should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional coffee machines, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.
Investment must be evaluated against the cost of development, distribution, and potential return on investment.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, small retail, or travel) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., semi‑automatic machines for home use) without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional coffee machines and existing distribution channels.
4) Partner with or license the professional technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Franke's own brand.

X1.name: Premium vs Eco Positioning Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions of a Franke consumer machine. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a premium positioning description (emphasizing professional quality, convenience, and modern design) or an eco‑friendly positioning description (emphasizing sustainability, water‑conserving features, and eco‑certification). After viewing the description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested) and state their top reason for choosing the machine.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers in Germany and Switzerland, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income to ensure representativeness.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (7‑point scale) and top reason for choosing the machine.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants exposed to the premium positioning description will report higher purchase intent and will cite taste and convenience as their top reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants exposed to the eco‑friendly positioning description will report higher purchase intent and will cite sustainability as their top reason.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for the premium positioning group is at least 1.5 points higher than for the eco‑friendly positioning group, and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), then T1 is supported. If the difference is not statistically significant, the test is inconclusive, and further evidence is needed.

frame.objective: Determine whether Franke Coffee Systems should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional coffee machines, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, small retail, or travel) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., semi‑automatic machines for home use) without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional coffee machines and existing distribution channels.
4) Partner with or license the professional technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Franke's own brand.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Franke would capture value through premium pricing, direct-to-consumer sales, and potential subscription services for maintenance or loyalty programs.

X1.measure: 1) Percentage of respondents choosing "time savings" vs "design/brand prestige" as primary purchase reason. 2) Average WTP premium (EUR) for each message. 3) Intent to purchase on a 7‑point scale (1‑"not likely" to 7‑"definite").

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Hoshizaki Corporation investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current commercial ice machines and kitchen equipment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home ice machines, portable refrigerators, or specialized kitchen equipment).
2) Expand the existing commercial product line into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., broader distribution of current commercial products).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current commercial ice machines and kitchen equipment business.
4) Change the route to buyers or customer group (e.g., shift from direct sales to retail partnerships or target a different demographic) without altering the product.

predictions: A test offering a differentiated ice machine will generate higher purchase intent or conversion than a standard commercial unit.

predictions: A branded differentiated ice machine will achieve higher average transaction value than an unbranded comparable unit.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Brand Premium
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a description of a differentiated ice machine emphasizing convenience and novelty (e.g., nugget ice, easy refilling). Group B sees the same description but emphasizes brand ownership and premium quality (e.g., Scotsman brand, reliability). Both groups see a price point (e.g., €150) and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question. After viewing the description, participants indicate their purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and state their maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 400 adult consumers in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced across both groups (200 per group).
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum price willingness to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent score and a higher average maximum price willingness to pay than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent score and a higher average maximum price willingness to pay than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience and novelty (supporting T1). If Group B's average purchase intent score is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A, proceed to develop a branded premium proposition (supporting T2). If the difference is less than 1.5 points, indicate uncertainty and recommend further market research.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes convenience and novelty (e.g., nugget ice, easy refilling). Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test to validate demand before committing to a full product launch. If the test shows a meaningful advantage for convenience, proceed with a convenience-focused product; otherwise, reassess the strategy.
final.target_customer: Home consumers who value convenience, novelty, and are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated ice experience.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated ice machine that delivers nugget ice and easy refilling, offering a unique, convenient experience that cannot be obtained from existing commercial or generic models.
final.next_action: Run the 12‑week, €20,000 Consumer Preference Test with 400 U.S. adults, comparing convenience‑focused and brand‑focused messaging. Use the 1.5‑point difference rule to decide whether to proceed with a convenience‑focused product or reassess
final.uncertainty: The test is the primary source of evidence; without it, consumer willingness to pay a premium for brand ownership remains uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows Group B’s purchase intent score is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A, indicating stronger demand for a branded premium proposition, we would shift focus to a branded premium strategy.
If the test shows no meaningful difference or a difference less than 1.5 points, we would recommend further market research before committing to a differentiated product.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Brand Premium
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a description of a differentiated ice machine emphasizing convenience and novelty (e.g., nugget ice, easy refilling). Group B sees the same description but emphasizes brand ownership and premium quality (e.g., Scotsman brand, reliability). Both groups see a price point (e.g., €150) and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question. After viewing the description, participants indicate their purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and state their maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 400 adult consumers in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced across both groups (200 per group).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum price willingness to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent score and a higher average maximum price willingness to pay than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent score and a higher average maximum price willingness to pay than Group A.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience and novelty (supporting T1). If Group B's average purchase intent score is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A, proceed to develop a branded premium proposition (supporting T2). If the difference is less than 1.5 points, indicate uncertainty and recommend further market research.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes convenience and novelty (e.g., nugget ice, easy refilling). Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test to validate demand before committing to a full product launch. If the test shows a meaningful advantage for convenience, proceed with a convenience-focused product; otherwise, reassess the strategy.

arguments.value_proposition: A differentiated ice machine that delivers nugget ice and easy refilling, offering a unique, convenient experience that cannot be obtained from existing commercial or generic models.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Hoshizaki Corporation investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current commercial ice machines and kitchen equipment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home ice machines, portable refrigerators, or specialized kitchen equipment).

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test for Home Ice Machine
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. residential consumers (aged 18-55) recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region.
X1.measure: 1) Purchase intent: "Would you purchase a home ice machine for personal use?" (binary: Yes/No). 2) WTP: "What is the maximum price you would pay for a home ice machine with a premium feature (e.g., nugget ice, unpasteurized ice, energy efficiency) compared to a standard commercial unit?" (price point). 3) Primary purchase driver: "Which of the following best describes why you would choose this ice machine?" (convenience, taste, health/wellness, other).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher WTP for a differentiated home ice machine than for a standard commercial unit, with convenience and taste as top drivers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher WTP for a health-focused home ice machine than for a differentiated home ice machine, with health/wellness as top driver.

X1.decision_rule: If the observed purchase intent for the differentiated home ice machine exceeds the standard commercial unit by at least 15 percentage points and the WTP is at least 20% higher than the standard unit, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 15 points or the WTP difference is less than 20%, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and consider other alternatives.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home ice machine) based on evidence of consumer demand for convenience and the existence of a differentiated market segment. Conduct a small-scale test (e.g., purchase intent survey) to validate demand before committing to full development. If the test shows a meaningful advantage, proceed; otherwise, consider other alternatives.
final.target_customer: Residential consumers aged 18-55 who value convenience, fresh ice, and are willing to pay a premium for premium features.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated home ice machine that offers convenience, high-quality nugget ice, and energy efficiency, sold through retail channels at a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (500 U.S. residential consumers, 6 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated home ice machine versus a standard commercial unit.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, the willingness to pay for premium features, and the ability to reach individual buyers through retail channels are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the differentiated home ice machine is at least 15 percentage points lower than for a standard commercial unit, or if willingness to pay is at least 20% lower, we would reconsider the investment.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand driven by health or unpasteurized ice, we would revise the theory and test a health-focused proposition.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test for Home Ice Machine
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. residential consumers (aged 18-55) recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region.
arguments.measure: 1) Purchase intent: "Would you purchase a home ice machine for personal use?" (binary: Yes/No). 2) WTP: "What is the maximum price you would pay for a home ice machine with a premium feature (e.g., nugget ice, unpasteurized ice, energy efficiency) compared to a standard commercial unit?" (price point). 3) Primary purchase driver: "Which of the following best describes why you would choose this ice machine?" (convenience, taste, health/wellness, other).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher WTP for a differentiated home ice machine than for a standard commercial unit, with convenience and taste as top drivers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher WTP for a health-focused home ice machine than for a differentiated home ice machine, with health/wellness as top driver.

arguments.decision_rule: If the observed purchase intent for the differentiated home ice machine exceeds the standard commercial unit by at least 15 percentage points and the WTP is at least 20% higher than the standard unit, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 15 points or the WTP difference is less than 20%, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and consider other alternatives.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home ice machine) based on evidence of consumer demand for convenience and the existence of a differentiated market segment. arguments.target_customer: Residential consumers aged 18-55 who value convenience, fresh ice, and are willing to pay a premium for premium features.
arguments.value_proposition: A differentiated home ice machine that offers convenience, high-quality nugget ice, and energy efficiency, sold through retail channels at a premium price.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (500 U.S. residential consumers, 6 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated home ice machine versus a standard commercial unit.
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, the willingness to pay for premium features, and the ability to reach individual buyers through retail channels are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the differentiated home ice machine is at least 15 percentage points lower than for a standard commercial unit, or if willingness to pay is at least 20% lower, we would reconsider the investment.

arguments.name: Differentiated Ice Machine Purchase Intent Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a differentiated ice machine versus a standard refrigerator ice unit. Participants view product descriptions and are asked to indicate purchase intent (1-7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect residential market.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR) for each product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the differentiated ice machine compared to the standard refrigerator ice unit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the differentiated ice machine that explicitly addresses a specific pain point (e.g., water waste, ice quality) compared to the standard refrigerator ice unit.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the differentiated ice machine exceeds the average purchase intent for the standard refrigerator ice unit by at least 1.5 points (e.g., 5.5 vs 4.0) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points or not statistically significant, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Hoshizaki Corporation investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current commercial ice machines and kitchen equipment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home ice machines, portable refrigerators, or specialized kitchen equipment).
2) Expand the existing commercial product line into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., broader distribution of current commercial products).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current commercial ice machines and kitchen equipment business.
4) Change the route to buyers or customer group (e.g., shift from direct sales to retail partnerships or target a different demographic) without altering the product.

T1.claim: Home consumers will adopt a differentiated ice machine if it offers a unique convenience feature (e.g., chewable ice, easy refilling) that cannot be obtained from existing commercial units.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking convenient, delicious ice at home; Hoshizaki benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand loyalty.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers currently buy commercial ice machines for fleet or large-scale use; a differentiated feature creates a new use case that justifies higher purchase cost.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Hoshizaki can price the differentiated unit above standard commercial units and sell through retail channels, earning margin on a new consumer segment.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a feature that improves convenience.
Hoshizaki can design and manufacture a differentiated unit without compromising commercial performance.
Retail distribution exists for a consumer-oriented unit.
predictions: A test offering a differentiated ice machine will generate higher purchase intent or sales than a standard commercial unit.
Surveyed consumers will rank convenience as the top reason for choosing the differentiated unit.

X1.name: Differentiated Ice Machine Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults (200 per arm) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income to reflect the target consumer segment.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum WTP (EUR) for each differentiated feature (convenience vs. water/energy efficiency).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the differentiated ice machine than for a standard commercial unit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the eco-featured ice machine than for a standard commercial unit.

X1.decision_rule: If the differentiated ice machine's purchase intent exceeds the standard commercial unit's intent by at least 10 percentage points and its WTP is at least 20% higher than the standard unit's WTP, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 10 points or the WTP difference is less than 20%, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.

revisions.reason: The simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer purchase intent, convenience features, or market demand for differentiated ice machines. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed purchase intent test (X1) to empirically compare differentiated ice machines with standard commercial units. If the test meets the decision threshold (10-point intent difference and ≥20% WTP difference), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience features. If the threshold is not met, do not invest in a differentiated proposition at this time.

final.next_action: Execute the 8‑week online survey test with 500 U.S. adults, measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for convenience versus eco features, and apply the decision threshold.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for differentiated ice machines, the willingness of consumers to pay a premium for convenience features, and the ability to reach retail channels without compromising commercial performance remain uncertain.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Tennant Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional floor-cleaning machines.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered from public sources.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage that would generate value for Tennant.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential home cleaning, small‑business cleaning, or a niche professional segment).
2) Expand the existing professional product line with new features or packaging without creating a separate consumer brand (e.g., premium branding, new accessories).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current professional market and existing distribution channels.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, subscription model, or partnership with retail chains) without altering the product.

T1.claim: Homeowners and small‑business owners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they increasingly view floor cleaning as a chore they can automate and because they value convenience and lower upfront cost, so a manufacturer that can deliver a compact, easy‑to‑use machine at a price they can afford will capture value through higher volume sales.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small‑business owners who need to clean hard floors without a full mopping system.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from manual mopping to a machine that does the work, reducing time and effort, and they are willing to pay a premium for a product that fits their space and budget.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tennant would sell a compact, low‑cost scrubber directly to consumers through retail channels, earning margin on each unit sold.
assumptions: Consumers currently avoid purchasing floor‑cleaning machines due to cost or perceived complexity.
A compact, easy‑to‑use machine meets the functional need of homeowners and small‑business owners.
Retail distribution can reach the target consumer base.
predictions: If offered a compact scrubber priced under $300, at least 10% of surveyed homeowners and small‑business owners will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales conversion rate will be higher in regions with higher home‑owning rates and lower average household income.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners and small‑business owners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they increasingly view floor cleaning as a chore they can automate and because they value convenience and lower upfront cost, so a manufacturer that can deliver a compact, easy‑to‑use machine at a price they can afford will capture value through higher volume sales.

T2.claim: Professional cleaning contractors will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they need a machine that performs at scale and is reliable for their business, so a manufacturer that can deliver a durable, high‑performance scrubber at a price that covers their operational costs will capture value through volume sales to distributors and through a professional‑focused brand.
T2.who_benefits: Professional cleaning contractors who need a machine that works for multiple jobs and is easy to maintain.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from using multiple tools to a single, reliable machine that reduces downtime and labor costs, and they are willing to pay a premium for durability and performance.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tennant would sell a professional‑grade scrubber through distributors at a higher margin, leveraging its existing distribution network to reach contractors.
assumptions: Professional contractors currently use multiple tools for different jobs, leading to higher operational costs.
A durable, high‑performance machine reduces downtime and labor costs.
Distributors are willing to stock a professional‑grade product at a premium price.
predictions: If offered a professional‑grade scrubber priced at $400‑$500, at least 15% of surveyed contractors will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales conversion will be higher in regions with higher contractor density and lower average contractor revenue per unit.

X1.name: Consumer vs Professional Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product offers and purchase intent questions.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners and small‑business owners (recruited via home‑owner panels) and 250 professional cleaning contractors (recruited via contractor panels).
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of respondents who say "Would buy" or "Would consider buying") for each product category (compact consumer scrubber vs professional‑grade scrubber).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners and small‑business owners will show higher purchase intent for the compact consumer scrubber than professional contractors.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Professional contractors will show higher purchase intent for the professional‑grade scrubber than homeowners and small‑business owners.

X1.decision_rule: If the purchase intent rate for the compact consumer scrubber among homeowners and small‑business owners is at least 15% higher than for the professional‑grade scrubber, conclude T1 is supported. If the purchase intent rate for the professional‑grade scrubber among professional contractors is at least 15% higher than for the compact consumer scrubber, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the 15‑point threshold, neither theory is supported.

final.recommendation: Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Professional Intent Test to empirically compare purchase intent for a compact consumer scrubber versus a professional‑grade scrubber. If the test meets the 15‑point threshold, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, maintain the current professional‑focused strategy and conduct further market research before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and small‑business owners who need to clean hard floors without a full mopping system.
final.value_proposition: A compact, easy‑to‑use floor scrubber priced under $300 that delivers high cleaning performance and fits small spaces, addressing the chore‑automation and convenience needs of consumers.
final.next_action: Run the 12‑week, €20,000 online survey test with 500 respondents (250 homeowners/small‑business owners, 250 contractors) to measure purchase intent for a compact consumer scrubber versus a professional‑grade scrubber.
final.uncertainty: The test results are pending; without the actual data, we cannot confirm whether consumers will purchase a differentiated product or whether professional contractors will adopt it.
would_change_if: If the test shows the compact consumer scrubber achieving a purchase intent rate at least 15 percentage points higher than the professional‑grade scrubber, we would shift toward developing a consumer proposition.

If the test shows the professional‑grade scrubber achieving a purchase intent rate at least 15 percentage points higher than the compact consumer scrubber, we would shift toward a professional‑focused strategy.
If neither difference meets the 15‑point threshold, we would recommend further market research before committing resources.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Professional Intent Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated product offers and purchase intent questions.
arguments.sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners and small‑business owners (recruited via home‑owner panels) and 250 professional cleaning contractors (recruited via contractor panels).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of respondents who say "Would buy" or "Would consider buying") for each product category (compact consumer scrubber vs professional‑grade scrubber).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners and small‑business owners will show higher purchase intent for the compact consumer scrubber than professional contractors.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Professional contractors will show higher purchase intent for the professional‑grade scrubber than homeowners and small‑business owners.

arguments.decision_rule: If the purchase intent rate for the compact consumer scrubber among homeowners and small‑business owners is at least 15% higher than for the professional‑grade scrubber, conclude T1 is supported. If the purchase intent rate for the professional‑grade scrubber among professional contractors is at least 15% higher than for the compact consumer scrubber, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the 15‑point threshold, neither theory is supported.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and higher average WTP for the premium convenience variant than for the sustainable variant.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small business owners will show higher purchase intent and higher average WTP for the sustainable variant than for the premium convenience variant.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium convenience variant's purchase intent among homeowners is at least 10 percentage points higher than the sustainable variant's, adopt T1. If neither difference meets the 10-point threshold, conclude insufficient evidence to favor either theory and recommend no expansion.

arguments.decision_rule: If the premium convenience variant's purchase intent among homeowners is at least 10 percentage points higher than the sustainable variant's, adopt T1. If neither difference meets the 10-point threshold, conclude insufficient evidence to favor either theory and recommend no expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Tennant Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional floor-cleaning machines.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑focused version of a professional scrubber in retail stores, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard professional model.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A (convenience messaging) or Condition B (sustainability messaging). Both conditions present a simplified version of a professional floor scrubber (e.g., compact, easy to use, small-space friendly) with a price point of €199. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions (250 per condition). Recruitment targets homeowners and small‑business owners in regions with high home‑owner density and small‑space housing.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (Condition A vs Condition B) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay in Condition B (sustainability messaging) compared to Condition A.

arguments.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Convenience vs Sustainability Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A (convenience messaging) or Condition B (sustainability messaging). Both conditions present a simplified version of a professional floor scrubber (e.g., compact, easy to use, small-space friendly) with a price point of €199. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
arguments.sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions (250 per condition). Recruitment targets homeowners and small‑business owners in regions with high home‑owner density and small‑space housing.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (Condition A vs Condition B) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay in Condition A (convenience messaging) compared to Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay in Condition B (sustainability messaging) compared to Condition A.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two conditions is at least 1.5 points (e.g., Condition A ≥ 6.5 and Condition B ≥ 5.0), conclude the respective theory is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home Cleaning Equipment
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners and small business owners. They are shown two product descriptions of the same equipment (e.g., a floor scrubber) with different messaging: one emphasizing convenience and sustainability (T1), and one emphasizing safety and hygiene (T2). Participants indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale and their purchase intent (1‑10).
X1.sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) recruited from a panel of homeowners and small business owners in the United States.
X1.measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent for the convenience/sustainability message compared to the safety message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent for the safety message compared to the convenience message.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the convenience message is at least 1.5 points higher than the average WTP for the safety message, conclude T1 is more likely to succeed. If the average WTP for the safety message is at least 1.5 points higher than the average WTP for the convenience message, conclude T2 is more likely to succeed. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the results are inconclusive and further testing is needed.

final.target_customer: Homeowners and small business owners seeking efficient, easy-to-use cleaning equipment that offers convenience and sustainability benefits.
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced, convenient, and sustainable home cleaning solution that delivers superior performance and reduces water usage, leveraging Tennant’s existing distribution network to reach individual buyers.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (300 participants, 12 weeks, €20,000) to compare willingness to pay and purchase intent for convenience vs. safety messaging.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the specific willingness to pay for differentiated features remain uncertain. The test will clarify whether consumers are willing to pay a premium for convenience and sustainability.
would_change_if: If the test shows the safety message achieving a 1.5-point higher average willingness to pay than the convenience message, T2 would become more likely to succeed and the recommendation would shift toward safety-focused messaging.
If the test yields no significant difference in willingness to pay between the two conditions, the results would be inconclusive and further market research would be needed.

predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced eco‑friendly floor scrubber, at least 30% of respondents will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.

predictions: In a test offering a compact, easy‑to‑use floor scrubber, at least 25% of respondents will report intent to purchase within 12 weeks.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Belimo Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current HVAC actuators, valves, and sensors, sold to commercial building manufacturers and through controls contractors and system integrators.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Belimo Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current HVAC actuators, valves, and sensors, sold to commercial building manufacturers and through controls contractors and system integrators.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must consider Belimo’s existing B2B business model and current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., residential home automation, DIY HVAC control, or a new consumer segment).
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio with new features or packaging without targeting consumers directly.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial building manufacturers and system integrators.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct-to-consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with home‑im improvement retailers, or a subscription model for home control services).
5) Target a different customer group within the commercial segment (e.g., small‑to‑medium office buildings, residential building owners, or energy‑efficient retrofits).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent will be at least 15% higher for the Belimo thermostat than for the generic equivalent, and WTP will be at least 20% higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent will be at least 10% higher for the Belimo thermostat than for the generic equivalent, and WTP will be at least 15% higher.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for Belimo exceeds the generic equivalent by 15% or more AND WTP exceeds the generic equivalent by 20% or more, conclude T1 is supported. If neither threshold is met, conclude no significant difference.

arguments.name: Residential HVAC Control Product Preference Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners who have purchased HVAC equipment in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum WTP (USD) for a Belimo residential thermostat at a 20% premium over a generic equivalent.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent will be at least 15% higher for the Belimo thermostat than for the generic equivalent, and WTP will be at least 20% higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent will be at least 10% higher for the Belimo thermostat than for the generic equivalent, and WTP will be at least 15% higher.

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent for Belimo exceeds the generic equivalent by 15% or more AND WTP exceeds the generic equivalent by 20% or more, conclude T1 is supported. If purchase intent for Belimo exceeds the generic equivalent by 10% or more AND WTP exceeds the generic equivalent by 15% or more, conclude T2 is supported. If neither threshold is met, conclude no significant difference.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for residential HVAC control that emphasizes energy efficiency and long-term cost savings, but first validate demand through a controlled test. X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and top reason for choosing the product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent and will cite safety and reliability as the top reason.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Belimo Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current HVAC actuators, valves, and sensors, sold to commercial building manufacturers and through controls contractors and system integrators.

5) Target a different customer group within the commercial segment (e.g., small‑to‑medium office buildings, residential building owners, or energy‑efficient retrofits).

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.

T1.claim: Home CPR training increases public awareness and willingness to intervene in cardiac arrest, leading individuals to purchase home training kits to prepare for emergencies. The perceived reduction of risk and the ability to act immediately create demand, which Laerdal can capture through direct-to-consumer sales of portable kits.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers who need to prepare for emergencies, and by extension, bystanders who might perform CPR in an emergency.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased public awareness of the importance of bystander CPR and the availability of easy-to-use home kits lowers the perceived risk and creates a perceived benefit, prompting individuals to own the training device.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal would capture value through premium-priced home CPR kits sold directly to consumers, generating revenue beyond B2B training programs.
assumptions: Consumers are aware of the importance of bystander CPR and are willing to invest in home training.
Home CPR kits are perceived as safe and effective for self-training.
Laerdal can reach and convert consumers effectively at a price point that justifies the investment.
predictions: In regions with high public awareness of bystander CPR, home CPR kit purchases will be higher than in regions with low awareness.

T2.claim: Consumers adopt home CPR training because it is marketed as a health and wellness product, aligning with personal fitness and self-care trends. This positioning attracts health-conscious individuals who view CPR training as part of their lifestyle, leading to purchase decisions driven by perceived personal benefit rather than emergency preparedness.
T2.who_benefits: Health-conscious consumers who seek to enhance personal wellness and are willing to invest in home health devices.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The integration of CPR training into a wellness narrative creates a personal benefit that motivates purchase, as consumers associate learning a life-saving skill with overall health improvement.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal would capture value through premium-priced home wellness kits sold directly to consumers, leveraging existing consumer marketing channels to reach health-conscious audiences.
assumptions: Consumers associate CPR training with personal health and wellness benefits.

predictions: In markets where wellness and self-care are prioritized, home CPR kit purchases will be higher than in markets where health concerns are less prominent.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home CPR Training
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) Personal Health Responsibility (PHR) condition: product described as a personal health responsibility to be learned at home; (2) Health Routine Condition: product described as part of a broader health routine and endorsed by trusted health authorities; (3) Control Condition: no product description. All participants are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay a premium (EUR).
X1.sample: 500 health-conscious adults recruited from an online panel, balanced across the three conditions.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay a premium (EUR) for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: PHR condition will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Health Routine and Control conditions.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Health Routine condition will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than PHR and Control conditions.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the PHR condition is at least 10 points higher than the average purchase intent in the Health Routine condition, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), then T1 is supported. If the average purchase intent in the Health Routine condition is at least 10 points higher than the average purchase intent in the PHR condition, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), then T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant, the test is inconclusive and no expansion is recommended.

arguments.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home CPR Training
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) Personal Health Responsibility (PHR) condition: product described as a personal health responsibility to be learned at home; (2) Health Routine Condition: product described as part of a broader health routine and endorsed by trusted health authorities; (3) Control Condition: no product description. All participants are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay a premium (EUR).
arguments.sample: 500 health-conscious adults recruited from an online panel, balanced across the three conditions.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay a premium (EUR) for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: PHR condition will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Health Routine and Control conditions.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Health Routine condition will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than PHR and Control conditions.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the PHR condition is at least 10 points higher than the average purchase intent in the Health Routine condition, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), then T1 is supported. If the average purchase intent in the Health Routine condition is at least 10 points higher than the average purchase intent in the PHR condition, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), then T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant, the test is inconclusive and no expansion is recommended.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home CPR Training
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious consumers (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups: Group A (safety/peace-of-mind messaging), Group B (health/wellness routine messaging), and Group C (control group without messaging). Each group views a product description of a home CPR training kit and is asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale.
X1.sample: 500 health-conscious consumers recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions.
X1.measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (percentage of participants indicating they would purchase the kit) for each messaging group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show the highest average WTP and purchase intent, as the safety/peace-of-mind message directly addresses life-saving motivation.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show the highest average WTP and purchase intent, as the health/wellness routine messaging aligns with existing consumer health habits.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A average WTP is at least 20 points higher than Group B and Group C, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), proceed to develop a safety/peace-of-mind consumer proposition. If Group B average WTP is at least 20 points higher than Group A and Group C, and the difference is statistically significant, develop a health/wellness routine proposition. If neither group meets the 20-point threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

arguments.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home CPR Training
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious consumers (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups: Group A (safety/peace-of-mind messaging), Group B (health/wellness routine messaging), and Group C (control group without messaging). Each group views a product description of a home CPR training kit and is asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale.
arguments.sample: 500 health-conscious consumers recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions.
arguments.measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (percentage of participants indicating they would purchase the kit) for each messaging group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show the highest average WTP and purchase intent, as the safety/peace-of-mind message directly addresses life-saving motivation.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show the highest average WTP and purchase intent, as the health/wellness routine messaging aligns with existing consumer health habits.

arguments.decision_rule: If Group A average WTP is at least 20 points higher than Group B and Group C, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), proceed to develop a safety/peace-of-mind consumer proposition. If Group B average WTP is at least 20 points higher than Group A and Group C, and the difference is statistically significant, develop a health/wellness routine proposition. If neither group meets the 20-point threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Laerdal already offers home CPR training (CPR Anytime) and has distributed kits to newborns, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or actual purchase behavior. A proposed test (Consumer Messaging Test) is needed to validate whether a safety/peace-of-mind proposition drives higher willingness to pay and purchase.

X1.name: Digital vs. Standalone Home CPR Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a safety-focused home CPR message (e.g., "Be prepared to save a life with home CPR training.") and Group B sees a convenience-focused home CPR message (e.g., "Learn CPR in 20 minutes with our portable kit."). Both groups view a product description of Laerdal’s home CPR kit and are asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale.
X1.sample: 500 health-conscious adults recruited from an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (on a 7-point scale). Secondary measure: share of participants indicating intent to purchase each message.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group B, because the safety message aligns with the perceived risk of cardiac arrest and the desire to be prepared.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group A, because the convenience message aligns with the desire for easy, data-backed wellness solutions.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the safety message is at least 1.5 times the average WTP for the convenience message (i.e., WTP_safety ≥ 1.5 × WTP_convenience), proceed to develop a safety-focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5, the convenience message is more promising and no expansion is recommended.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kingspan Group plc investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B insulation and building envelope products.

Evidence must demonstrate consumer willingness to purchase, current market size, and potential value capture for Kingspan.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., homeowner DIY insulation, small‑scale building retrofits).
2) Expand the existing B2B insulation and building envelope products into new professional segments (e.g., larger construction firms, public‑building contractors).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market without introducing a consumer proposition.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups: Group A (government‑approved, SEAI One Stop Shop messaging), Group B (premium performance messaging), and Group C (neutral control). Each group views a product description of Kingspan insulation and is asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not likely to 7‑very likely).
X1.sample: 300 UK homeowners (150 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑to 7) for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have the highest average purchase intent score (≈5.5) due to trust in government funding and the SEAI One Stop Shop process.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have the highest average purchase intent score (≈5.5) due to premium performance messaging, even without government funding.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B, conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant, conclude neither theory is strongly supported.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kingspan Group plc investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B insulation and building envelope products.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., homeowner DIY insulation, small‑scale building retrofits).

3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market without introducing a consumer proposition.
4) Partner with existing consumer brands or retailers to bring Kingspan products to individual buyers (e.g., retail distribution of insulation panels).
5) License the insulation technology to consumer‑focused manufacturers rather than selling under the Kingspan brand.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Kingspan can capture value by pricing the product competitively, offering financial incentives (e.g., cashback or grant partnerships), and leveraging its existing distribution channels to reach consumers directly or through retailers.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Energy Savings vs Brand Trust
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of UK homeowners (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Condition A emphasizes energy savings and financial return on investment (ROI) of insulation. Condition B emphasizes brand trust, safety, and compliance with building regulations. After viewing the product description and price, participants indicate their likelihood to purchase (1‑10 scale) and the maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 UK homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two message conditions.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (likelihood to buy) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition A.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 10 points (e.g., 60% vs 50%), we conclude T1 is supported. If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least 10 points, we conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 points, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend further testing.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (X1) to empirically compare energy‑saving messaging versus brand trust messaging on purchase intent and willingness to pay. If the test shows a ≥10‑point difference in favor of energy‑saving messaging, develop a consumer proposition emphasizing ROI. If the difference is <10 points, conduct additional testing or consider a partner‑led approach before committing to a full launch
final.target_customer: UK homeowners and building owners seeking to reduce energy bills and improve home comfort.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that highlights the financial return on investment (ROI) of Kingspan's home insulation products, positioning them as a cost‑effective upgrade that delivers measurable savings.
final.next_action: Execute the 6‑week, €18,000 Consumer Messaging Test (X1) with 500 UK homeowners, randomized to energy‑saving vs brand trust messaging, and analyze results against the 10‑point threshold.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources; no direct consumer purchase data exists. The test will resolve whether energy‑saving messaging or brand trust messaging drives higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥10‑point difference in favor of brand trust messaging, we would shift focus to emphasizing quality, safety, and compliance as the primary value proposition.
If neither message shows a ≥10‑point difference, we would recommend further testing or a partner‑led approach before committing to a consumer launch.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kingspan Group plc investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B insulation and building envelope products.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Need to identify existing consumer reach (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales, retail partnerships) and demand for a differentiated product.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer willingness to purchase, current market size, and potential value capture for Kingspan.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., homeowner DIY insulation, small‑scale building retrofits).
2) Expand the existing B2B insulation and building envelope products into new professional segments (e.g., larger construction firms, public‑building contractors).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market without introducing a consumer proposition.
4) Partner with existing consumer brands or retailers to bring Kingspan products to individual buyers (e.g., retail distribution of insulation panels).
5) License the insulation technology to consumer‑focused manufacturers rather than selling under the Kingspan brand.

predictions: In regions with active SEAI grant programs, homeowner uptake of Kingspan insulation will be higher than in regions without such programs.

predictions: In markets where energy efficiency is a primary purchase driver, homeowners will show higher willingness to pay for Kingspan insulation compared to generic alternatives.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kingspan Group plc investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B insulation and building envelope products.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., homeowner DIY insulation, small‑scale building retrofits).

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kingspan Group plc investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B insulation and building envelope products.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., homeowner DIY insulation, small‑scale building retrofits).
2) Expand the existing B2B insulation and building envelope products into new professional segments (e.g., larger construction firms, public‑building contractors).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market without introducing a consumer proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether Ansell Limited should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial and healthcare protective gloves and body protection, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources for evidence; internal financial or contractual details may not be public.

Current consumer reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, cycling, gardening) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand the existing product portfolio into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., general protective gloves for everyday use).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on industrial and healthcare segments, leveraging existing relationships and distribution.
4) Partner with or license the Ansell brand to third‑party consumer brands for existing protective gear, capturing value through royalties or co‑branding.

arguments.name: Differentiated Glove Purchase Intent Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a differentiated outdoor‑recreation glove versus a generic glove, followed by a willingness‑to‑pay question.
arguments.sample: 500 respondents recruited from outdoor recreation and cycling interest panels, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willing to pay for the differentiated glove.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the differentiated glove will be at least 15% higher than for the generic glove, and the average willingness‑to‑pay will be at least 20% higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the differentiated glove will be at least 20% higher than for the generic glove, and the average willingness‑to‑pay will be at least 20% higher.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the differentiated and generic glove is at least 15 percentage points and the difference in willingness‑to‑pay is at least 20%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference in purchase intent is less than 15 points or the difference in willingness‑to‑pay is less than 20%, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether Ansell Limited should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial and healthcare protective gloves and body protection, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, cycling, gardening) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand the existing product portfolio into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., general protective gloves for everyday use).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on industrial and healthcare segments, leveraging existing relationships and distribution.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Differentiated Glove Proposition
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of consumers who have purchased protective gloves in the past 12 months. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three message conditions: (1) lifestyle/fashion positioning (e.g., "These gloves are designed for outdoor adventures and look great on your hands."), (2) activity-specific necessity positioning (e.g., "These gloves are essential for gardening, cycling, and outdoor work where protection matters."), and (3) neutral control (no positioning). After viewing the message, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").
X1.sample: 300 participants (100 per condition) to ensure statistical power and representativeness.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition 1 will achieve the highest average purchase intent score and WTP, indicating strong lifestyle/fashion appeal.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition 2 will achieve the highest average purchase intent score and WTP, indicating strong activity-specific necessity appeal.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Condition 1 is at least 1.5 points higher than Condition 2, proceed with a differentiated lifestyle/fashion proposition. If Condition 2 is at least 1.5 points higher, proceed with an activity-specific necessity proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, no expansion is recommended.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (X1) to empirically compare lifestyle/fashion versus activity-specific necessity positioning. If Condition 1 achieves at least a 1.5-point higher purchase intent score than Condition 2, proceed with a differentiated lifestyle/fashion proposition. If Condition 2 wins, pursue an activity-specific necessity prop
final.target_customer: Individual consumers who purchase protective gloves for lifestyle, outdoor, or activity-specific purposes.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions gloves as a stylish, lifestyle accessory or essential tool for specific activities, offering unique design, brand storytelling, and activity-specific features.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Messaging Test (300 participants, 8 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under lifestyle and activity-specific messaging.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer perception and willingness to pay. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows Condition 2 achieving at least a 1.5-point higher purchase intent score than Condition 1, indicating strong activity-specific necessity appeal, the recommendation would shift to an activity-specific necessity proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference (<1.5 points) between the two conditions, no expansion would be recommended.

arguments.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Differentiated Glove Proposition
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of consumers who have purchased protective gloves in the past 12 months. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three message conditions: (1) lifestyle/fashion positioning (e.g., "These gloves are designed for outdoor adventures and look great on your hands."), (2) activity-specific necessity positioning (e.g., "These gloves are essential for gardening, cycling, and outdoor work where protection matters."), and (3) neutral control (no positioning). After viewing the message, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").
arguments.sample: 300 participants (100 per condition) to ensure statistical power and representativeness.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

X1.name: Specialized vs Lifestyle Glove Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized product exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions to ensure representativeness.
X1.measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary choice (would buy the specialized glove vs the lifestyle-branded glove). 2) WTP: maximum price consumers would pay for each glove. 3) Primary reason for choosing (open-ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Specialized glove will have higher purchase intent and higher WTP than lifestyle-branded glove, with consumers citing protection and performance as the primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Lifestyle-branded glove will have higher purchase intent and higher WTP than specialized glove, with consumers citing personal branding and identity as the primary reason.

X1.decision_rule: If the specialized glove achieves purchase intent ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €15 (above the average WTP of €12 for the lifestyle-branded glove), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case. If the lifestyle-branded glove achieves purchase intent ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €15, develop a lifestyle-branded consumer proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand into consumer markets.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. The evidence does not provide sufficient proof that consumers will adopt differentiated gloves for specific use cases or that they will pay a premium. A small-scale willingness-to-pay test (as proposed in test X1) would be needed to validate demand before any investment.
final.target_customer: Outdoor enthusiasts, cyclists, gardeners, and consumers seeking specialized protection who currently rely on generic or generic-like gloves.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated protective glove for a specific use case that offers superior protection and performance, positioned as a premium, specialized item.
final.next_action: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay test (X1) to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity before any product development.
final.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for specialized gloves and the extent to which personal branding drives purchase decisions remain uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 60% or average willingness-to-pay below €15, the case for a consumer proposition would weaken and further testing or a different approach would be considered.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for lifestyle-branded gloves or a clear willingness-to-pay premium, the recommendation would shift toward a lifestyle-branded consumer proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether Ansell Limited should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial and healthcare protective gloves and body protection, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources for evidence; internal financial or contractual details may not be public.
