alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, cycling, gardening) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand the existing product portfolio into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., general protective gloves for everyday use).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on industrial and healthcare segments, leveraging existing relationships and distribution.
4) Partner with or license the Ansell brand to third‑party consumer brands for existing protective gear, capturing value through royalties or co‑branding.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Ansell protective gloves for specific use cases (e.g., outdoor recreation, cycling, gardening) if they perceive the gloves as high‑performance, reliable, and differentiated from generic consumer gloves.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers who need reliable protection for activities where existing consumer gloves fail.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers will switch to a differentiated Ansell brand if they experience superior protection, durability, and comfort compared to standard consumer gloves.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can charge premium prices for the differentiated consumer line and capture value through direct‑to‑consumer sales and brand equity.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for protected gloves when performance is clear.
The differentiated features (e.g., material, design) are distinct enough from existing consumer gloves.
Distribution channels (e.g., specialty outdoor retailers) exist for the target use case.
predictions: A test offering a differentiated outdoor‑recreation glove will generate higher conversion rates than an identical non‑differentiated glove.
Surveyed consumers will report higher satisfaction with the differentiated glove than with standard consumer gloves.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can price the consumer line at a premium and capture value through limited‑edition collaborations, brand licensing, and direct‑to‑consumer sales channels that emphasize prestige.
assumptions: Brand perception of Ansell as a trusted industrial/healthcare protector transfers to consumer perception.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a brand they associate with quality and professionalism.
The target use case (e.g., cycling, gardening) has a segment of consumers who value status and are willing to pay for it.
predictions: A test offering a differentiated glove with a prestige‑focused marketing campaign will achieve higher purchase intent than an identical glove without such messaging.

X1.name: Differentiated vs Prestige Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and purchase intent measurement.
X1.sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across three groups: 200 see a differentiated outdoor‑recreation glove description, 200 see a prestige‑focused description, and 100 see a neutral functional description.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary: self‑reported importance of protection vs prestige.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group seeing differentiated description will have higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than the prestige group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group seeing prestige description will have higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than the differentiated group.

X1.decision_rule: If the differentiated group achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and its willingness to pay is at least 20% above the prestige group, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the prestige group achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and its willingness to pay is at least 20% above the differentiated group, develop a prestige‑focused proposition. If neither group meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer markets.

final.next_action: Execute the 8‑week, €18,000 test with 500 consumers, measure purchase intent and willingness to pay, and apply the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer line.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test for Specialized vs Lifestyle Glove
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product concepts: (1) Specialized glove for outdoor recreation (e.g., durable, waterproof, stylish design) and (2) Lifestyle-branded glove positioned as a fashion accessory aligned with personal style. Participants view product images and are asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10).
X1.sample: 500 adult consumers aged 18–45 who have purchased protective gloves in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel to ensure diversity in gender, age, and geographic location.
X1.measure: Average WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (percentage) for each concept.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent for the specialized glove compared to the lifestyle-branded glove.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent for the lifestyle-branded glove compared to the specialized glove.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the specialized glove is at least 20% higher than for the lifestyle-branded glove, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for outdoor recreation. If the lifestyle-branded glove's WTP is at least 20% higher, develop a lifestyle-branded consumer proposition. If neither difference meets the 20% threshold, do not invest in either proposition.

arguments.measure: Average WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (percentage) for each concept.

frame.objective: Determine whether Ansell Limited should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial and healthcare protective gloves and body protection, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources for evidence; internal financial or contractual details may not be public.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, cycling, gardening) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand the existing product portfolio into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., general protective gloves for everyday use).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on industrial and healthcare segments, leveraging existing relationships and distribution.
4) Partner with or license the Ansell brand to third‑party consumer brands for existing protective gear, capturing value through royalties or co‑branding.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt differentiated protective gloves for specific use cases (e.g., outdoor recreation, cycling, gardening) if they perceive the product as a premium, specialized item that offers superior protection and style, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking specialized protection for activities where standard gloves fail.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Shifting from generic industrial gloves to purpose-built, stylish gloves creates a perceived value that justifies higher price and multiple purchases.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can capture value through premium pricing, brand differentiation, and potential licensing of the specialized design to third-party consumer brands.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for specialized protective gear.
The differentiated product can be produced at scale without compromising quality.
The brand can be effectively positioned as premium and specialized in the consumer market.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a specialized glove compared to standard gloves.
Purchase intent for the specialized glove will be higher among consumers who engage in outdoor activities than among those who do not.
Repeat purchase rate for the specialized glove will be higher than for standard gloves.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt differentiated protective gloves for specific use cases (e.g., outdoor recreation, cycling, gardening) if they perceive the product as a premium, specialized item that offers superior protection and style, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt differentiated protective gloves for specific use cases if they perceive the product as a health and safety requirement, leading to purchase driven by compliance and regulatory standards rather than style or premium positioning.
T2.who_benefits: Healthcare professionals, industrial workers, and regulatory entities requiring compliant protective gear.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Compliance and regulatory mandates increase the perceived necessity of protective gloves, prompting purchases even if the product is not perceived as stylish or premium.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can capture value through higher volume sales to industrial and healthcare segments, potential licensing of compliant designs, and partnerships with regulatory bodies.
assumptions: Regulatory compliance is a primary driver for purchase decisions in the target segments.
The differentiated product meets or exceeds the required standards without compromising functionality.
The brand can be effectively positioned as compliant and reliable in the consumer market.
predictions: Purchase intent for the differentiated glove will be higher among buyers who must comply with specific safety standards than among buyers who purchase for non-compliance reasons.
Sales of the differentiated glove will be concentrated in regions with strict safety regulations.
Repeat purchase rate will be lower than for standard gloves due to the compliance-driven nature of the purchase.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Specialized Glove Proposition
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 adult consumers recruited from outdoor recreation, cycling, and gardening interest lists, balanced across gender and age.
X1.measure: Average WTP in euros for a specialized glove (e.g., outdoor recreation) versus a standard glove, and self-reported purchase intent on a 7-point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP for the specialized glove (e.g., €15-20) and higher purchase intent among outdoor-recreation participants than among non-participants.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP for the specialized glove (e.g., €15-20) and higher purchase intent among buyers who cite compliance (e.g., OSHA, ISO) than among buyers who cite style or premium positioning.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the specialized glove exceeds the average WTP for the standard glove by at least €5 and the purchase intent among outdoor-recreation participants exceeds that among non-participants by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the WTP difference is less than €5 or the purchase intent difference is less than 10 percentage points, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.

arguments.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Specialized Glove Proposition
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 500 adult consumers recruited from outdoor recreation, cycling, and gardening interest lists, balanced across gender and age.
arguments.measure: Average WTP in euros for a specialized glove (e.g., outdoor recreation) versus a standard glove, and self-reported purchase intent on a 7-point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP for the specialized glove (e.g., €15-20) and higher purchase intent among outdoor-recreation participants than among non-participants.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP for the specialized glove (e.g., €15-20) and higher purchase intent among buyers who cite compliance (e.g., OSHA, ISO) than among buyers who cite style or premium positioning.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the specialized glove exceeds the average WTP for the standard glove by at least €5 and the purchase intent among outdoor-recreation participants exceeds that among non-participants by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the WTP difference is less than €5 or the purchase intent difference is less than 10 percentage points, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Mettler-Toledo can charge a premium for precision features and sell through direct channels, leveraging its brand reputation for accuracy.

Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a precision digital scale to home cooks, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard digital scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for Precision messaging than for Health messaging.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Mettler-Toledo International Inc. investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food weighing, personal fitness, or small‑business retail).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio by adding new industrial or laboratory applications without a consumer focus.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a precision tool for accurate ingredient measurement, because they value repeatable results for cooking and food preparation.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks and food preparers who need reliable weight measurement for recipes and portion control.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Current consumer scales lack precision; a scale that measures by weight reliably reduces guesswork and improves recipe accuracy.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Mettler-Toledo can charge a premium for precision features and sell through direct channels, leveraging its brand reputation for accuracy.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for precision over basic features.
Marketing can effectively communicate the precision benefit to home users.
Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a precision digital scale to home cooks, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard digital scale.
Willingness to pay will be above the price of a standard scale by at least 20%.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a precision tool for accurate ingredient measurement, because they value repeatable results for cooking and food preparation.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a health and wellness tool for portion control and carbohydrate counting, because they seek tools that support dietary goals.
T2.who_benefits: Individuals following specific diets (e.g., low-carb, keto) and health-conscious consumers.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers already use digital scales for weight monitoring and want a tool that directly supports their dietary objectives.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Mettler-Toledo can position the scale as a health companion, justify a premium price, and sell through direct channels or specialty retailers.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for features that directly support their diet.
Marketing can effectively link the scale to health and wellness messaging.
Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a health-focused digital scale, purchase intent will be higher than for a precision-focused scale.
Willingness to pay will be above the price of a precision scale by at least 15%.

X1.name: Precision vs Health Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants view one of two product descriptions for a digital kitchen scale: Precision (accurate, fraction-of-a-gram measurement) or Health (portion control, carbohydrate counting). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay (open-ended).
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age. Randomly assigned to see Precision or Health messaging.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum price willingness to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for Precision messaging than for Health messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for Health messaging than for Precision messaging.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for Precision messaging is at least 20% higher than for Health messaging, conclude T1 is more supported. If the difference is less than 20%, conclude T2 is more supported. If both differences are within 20% of each other, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Precision vs Health messaging test to empirically compare consumer demand for precision versus health-focused messaging. If the test shows a ≥20% difference in willingness to pay for Precision messaging, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing precision. If the difference is within 20% or inconclusive, conduct additional market research before committing to a full product
final.target_customer: Home cooks and food preparers who need reliable weight measurement for recipes and portion control.
final.value_proposition: A precision digital kitchen scale that measures by weight with fraction-of-a-gram accuracy, marketed as the only way to ensure predictable results in cooking.
final.next_action: Execute the 12‑week, €2,000 Precision vs Health messaging test with 300 adult consumers, randomized to see Precision or Health messaging, and analyze willingness to pay and purchase intent.
final.uncertainty: The test is the primary source of evidence; without it, consumer demand for precision is unknown. The test may not capture all consumer motivations, and willingness to pay may be influenced by factors not measured.
would_change_if: If the test shows a <20% difference in willingness to pay between Precision and Health messaging, indicating no clear consumer preference, or if additional research reveals strong demand for health-focused features, the recommendation would
shift toward developing a health‑focused consumer proposition.

arguments.name: Precision vs Health Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants view one of two product descriptions for a digital kitchen scale: Precision (accurate, fraction-of-a-gram measurement) or Health (portion control, carbohydrate counting). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay (open-ended).
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age. Randomly assigned to see Precision or Health messaging.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum price willingness to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for Precision messaging than for Health messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for Health messaging than for Precision messaging.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for Precision messaging is at least 20% higher than for Health messaging, conclude T1 is more supported. If the difference is less than 20%, conclude T2 is more supported. If both differences are within 20% of each other, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Run the proposed Precision vs Health messaging test to empirically compare consumer demand for precision versus health-focused messaging. X1.name: Precision vs Health Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants view one of two product descriptions for a digital kitchen scale: Precision (accurate, fraction-of-a-gram measurement) or Health (portion control, carbohydrate counting). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay (open-ended).
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age. Randomly assigned to see Precision or Health messaging.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum price willingness to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for Precision messaging than for Health messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for Health messaging than for Precision messaging.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for Precision messaging is at least 20% higher than for Health messaging, conclude T1 is more supported. If the difference is less than 20%, conclude T2 is more supported. If both differences are within 20% of each other, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Precision vs Health messaging test to empirically compare consumer demand for precision versus health-focused messaging. If the test shows a ≥20% difference in willingness to pay for Precision messaging, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing precision. If the difference is within 20% or inconclusive, conduct additional market research before committing to a full product
final.target_customer: Home cooks and food preparers who need reliable weight measurement for recipes and portion control.
final.value_proposition: A precision digital kitchen scale that measures by weight with fraction-of-a-gram accuracy, marketed as the only way to ensure predictable results in cooking.
final.next_action: Execute the 12‑week, €2,000 Precision vs Health messaging test with 300 adult consumers, randomized to see Precision or Health messaging, and analyze willingness to pay and purchase intent.
final.uncertainty: The test is the primary source of evidence; without it, consumer demand for precision is unknown. The test may not capture all consumer motivations, and willingness to pay may be influenced by factors not measured.
would_change_if: If the test shows a <20% difference in willingness to pay between Precision and Health messaging, indicating no clear consumer preference, or if additional research reveals strong demand for health-focused features, the recommendation would
shift toward developing a health‑focused consumer proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Mettler-Toledo International Inc. investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current sales are primarily through direct sales force; indirect channels are unknown.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a differentiated product.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food weighing, personal fitness, or small‑business retail).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio by adding new industrial or laboratory applications without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B customers and existing sales channels.
4) Change the sales route to reach individual buyers directly (e.g., e‑commerce, subscription model) without altering the product.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a precision tool for accurate ingredient measurement, because they value repeatable results for cooking and food preparation.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks and food preparers who need reliable weight measurement for recipes and portion control.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Current consumer scales lack precision; a scale that measures by weight reliably reduces guesswork and improves recipe accuracy.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Mettler-Toledo can charge a premium for precision features and sell through direct channels, leveraging its brand reputation for accuracy.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for precision over basic features.
Marketing can effectively communicate the precision benefit to home users.
Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a precision digital scale to home cooks, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard digital scale.
Willingness to pay will be above the price of a standard scale by at least 20%.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers already use digital scales for weight monitoring and want a tool that directly supports their dietary objectives.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Mettler-Toledo can position the scale as a health companion, justify a premium price, and sell through direct channels or specialty retailers.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for features that directly support their diet.
Marketing can effectively link the scale to health and wellness messaging.
Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a health-focused digital scale, purchase intent will be higher than for a precision-focused scale.
Willingness to pay will be above the price of a precision scale by at least 15%.

X1.name: Precision vs Health Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants view one of two product descriptions for a digital kitchen scale: Precision (accurate, fraction-of-a-gram measurement) or Health (portion control, carbohydrate counting). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age. Randomly assigned to see Precision or Health messaging.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for Precision messaging than for Health messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for Health messaging than for Precision messaging.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for Precision messaging is at least 20% higher than for Health messaging (EUR), proceed to develop a precision‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20%, proceed to develop a health‑focused proposition. If both differences are within 20% of each other, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

arguments.name: Precision vs Health Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants view one of two product descriptions for a digital kitchen scale: Precision (accurate, fraction-of-a-gram measurement) or Health (portion control, carbohydrate counting). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay (EUR).
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age. Randomly assigned to see Precision or Health messaging.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for Precision messaging than for Health messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for Health messaging than for Precision messaging.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for Precision messaging is at least 20% higher than for Health messaging (EUR), proceed to develop a precision‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20%, proceed to develop a health‑focused proposition. If both differences are within 20% of each other, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Mettler-Toledo International Inc. investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current sales are primarily through direct sales force; indirect channels are unknown.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a differentiated product.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food weighing, personal fitness, or small‑business retail).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio by adding new industrial or laboratory applications without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B customers and existing sales channels.
4) Change the sales route to reach individual buyers directly (e.g., e‑commerce, subscription model) without altering the product.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a precision tool for accurate ingredient measurement, because they value repeatable results for cooking and food preparation.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks and food preparers who need reliable weight measurement for recipes and portion control.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Current consumer scales lack precision; a scale that measures by weight reliably reduces guesswork and improves recipe accuracy.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Mettler-Toledo can charge a premium for precision features and sell through direct channels, leveraging its brand reputation for accuracy.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for precision over basic features.
Marketing can effectively communicate the precision benefit to home users.
Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a precision digital scale to home cooks, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard digital scale.
Willingness to pay will be above the price of a standard scale by at least 20%.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers already use digital scales for weight monitoring and want a tool that directly supports their dietary objectives.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Mettler-Toledo can position the scale as a health companion, justify a premium price, and sell through direct channels or specialty retailers.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for features that directly support their diet.
Marketing can effectively link the scale to health and wellness messaging.
Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a health-focused digital scale, purchase intent will be higher than for a precision-focused scale.
Willingness to pay will be above the price of a precision scale by at least 15%.

X1.name: Precision vs Health Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants view one of two product descriptions for a digital kitchen scale: Precision (accurate, fraction-of-a-gram measurement) or Health (portion control, carbohydrate counting). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age. Randomly assigned to see Precision or Health messaging.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for Precision messaging than for Health messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for Health messaging than for Precision messaging.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for Precision messaging is at least 20% higher than for Health messaging (EUR), proceed to develop a precision‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20%, proceed to develop a health‑focused proposition. If both differences are within 20% of each other, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

X1.name: Precision vs Health Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants view one of two product descriptions for a digital kitchen scale: Precision (accurate, fraction-of-a-gram measurement) or Health (portion control, carbohydrate counting). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age. Randomly assigned to see Precision or Health messaging.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for Precision messaging than for Health messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for Health messaging than for Precision messaging.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for Precision messaging is at least 20% higher than for Health messaging (EUR), proceed to develop a precision‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20%, proceed to develop a health‑focused proposition. If both differences are within 20% of each other, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

arguments.name: Precision vs Health Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants view one of two product descriptions for a digital kitchen scale: Precision (accurate, fraction-of-a-gram measurement) or Health (portion control, carbohydrate counting). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay (EUR).
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age. Randomly assigned to see Precision or Health messaging.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for Precision messaging than for Health messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for Health messaging than for Precision messaging.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for Precision messaging is at least 20% higher than for Health messaging (EUR), proceed to develop a precision‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20%, proceed to develop a health‑focused proposition. If both differences are within 20% of each other, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.
